content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a baked product made from dough of flour, water, yeast (or sourdough starter) and salt. It can be homemade following a recipe or purchased from a bakery. Often served toasted, which gives a crunchy crust and a rich aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bread is one of the oldest foods, baked already in ancient Egypt.
There are more than 200 varieties of bread, differing in shape, flavor and leavening method.
Toasting enhances flavor through the Maillard reaction.
In many cultures bread symbolizes hospitality and prosperity.
Stale bread is commonly repurposed into breadcrumbs, croutons and bread pudding.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides steady energy thanks to slowly digestible carbs that help maintain blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain bread supplies thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber (when whole‑grain)
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bread provides iron, magnesium and zinc, important for blood formation and immune function.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Sourdough bread contains probiotic bacteria that may benefit the intestinal flora.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience inflammation and discomfort after eating bread.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood sugar quickly, which can be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some breads contain high amounts of salt, potentially contributing to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercially produced loaves may include additives that can trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be eaten fresh, toasted, as sandwiches, croutons, served with soups, or used to make breadcrumbs and stuffing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag; thaw and toast before use.

chow-mein-or-chop-suey-meatless-with-noo.title: Meatless Chow Mein or Chop Suey with Noodles

content.title: About
content.content: Chow mein and chop suey are popular Asian dishes made with stir‑fried noodles, vegetables, and soy‑based sauces. In the meatless version they contain tofu, mushrooms or soy protein instead of meat, making them a flavorful and nutritious option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow mein was introduced to the United States in the early 1920s when Chinese immigrants adapted the traditional recipe to local tastes.
Chop suey is often called “Chinese hash” because it combines a variety of vegetables, sauces, and sometimes rice.
Vegetarian versions use soy sauce, mushroom “oyster” sauce and spices to recreate the umami flavor of meat.
Traditional chow mein uses thin egg noodles, but vegetarian recipes often use whole‑grain or rice noodles.
Both dishes scale easily—from a quick single‑serving lunch to a family‑style dinner.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Tofu, soy chunks and mushrooms provide a complete amino‑acid profile that supports muscle maintenance and metabolism.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables such as broccoli, carrots and bell peppers, together with whole‑grain noodles, aid digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of meat and the use of vegetable oils make the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Broccoli, carrots and mushrooms supply vitamin C, vitamin K, potassium and iron.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Soy sauce and mushrooms contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu and other soy products can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is often high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some pre‑made sauces contain added MSG, which may cause headaches in certain people.

items.title: Noodle quality
items.content: Overcooked or undercooked noodles can affect texture and digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, straight from the wok. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime wedges or sliced chili for extra zing. Add extra soy sauce, toasted sesame oil or a nut‑based sauce if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat with a splash of oil or water to keep the noodles from drying out.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-dry-mix-made-with-wa.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa, dry mix, made with water

content.title: About
content.content: The dry mix for hot chocolate is a blend of cocoa powder, sugar, and flavorings. When mixed with hot water it yields a rich, aromatic beverage that is quick to prepare and does not require milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix often contains a small amount of emulsifiers to keep the drink smooth and free of sediment.
Cocoa powder in dry mixes is usually roasted at low temperatures to preserve volatile aroma compounds.
In some countries hot chocolate is spiced with cinnamon or vanilla for a more complex flavor.
Dry mixes are convenient for travel and camping – just add boiling water.
Cocoa is rich in flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Rich in flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids help improve vascular function and act as antioxidants.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Cocoa contains theobromine and small amounts of caffeine, which can boost alertness and improve mood.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The mix provides magnesium, iron, and potassium, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Cognitive benefits
items.content: Moderate regular consumption of cocoa has been linked to better memory and concentration.

items.title: Easy portion control
items.content: Because the drink is made from a measured dry mix, sugar and calorie intake can be easily regulated.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Most dry mixes contain added sugar, which can be an issue for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to cocoa or added flavorings.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Although present in low amounts, sensitive individuals may experience insomnia or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Cocoa can increase stomach acidity, so people with gastritis should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Dissolve 2‑3 tablespoons of the dry mix in 200‑250 ml of hot (but not boiling) water, stirring until smooth. Optionally add milk, cream, or a sweetener.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Discard if clumps form or the product develops an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb is the meat of young sheep. The NS (as to cut) format provides thinly sliced pieces ready for quick cooking. The meat has a distinctive aroma, tender flavor, and a slight sweet note typical of lamb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is one of the oldest meats consumed by humans.
It features in many traditional dishes worldwide, from Mediterranean kebabs to Indian curries.
NS cuts are ideal for fast‑cook recipes such as stir‑fry, kebabs, and salads.
Sheep grazing on grass give the meat higher levels of omega‑3 fatty acids.
Lamb contains more iron than beef, making it a valuable source of this mineral.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Lamb provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: The iron in lamb is highly bioavailable and supports normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc aids immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lamb.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive consumption can contribute to elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking may allow pathogenic bacteria to grow.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Lamb is rich in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: NS‑cut lamb is convenient for grilling, pan‑searing, or wok cooking. Add it to salads, pasta, rice dishes, or use as a sandwich filling. A brief marination in olive oil with herbs enhances flavor before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sliced lamb in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Discard any meat with off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated diet cola is a carbonated soft drink flavored like classic cola, containing no caffeine and no sugar. It provides the familiar cola taste for those who want to limit calories and caffeine intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Diet colas first appeared in the 1960s as a response to the growing diet trend.
The decaffeinated version is usually made by removing caffeine from regular cola syrup.
It typically contains artificial sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose.
Carbonated water enhances the perception of flavor without adding calories.
While some brands use natural flavorings, most rely on synthetic ingredients.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Diet cola provides virtually zero calories, helping with energy balance control.

items.title: Caffeine-free
items.content: Suitable for individuals sensitive to caffeine or who limit its intake.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any water, it contributes to daily fluid needs.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some people may experience sensitivity to aspartame or sucralose.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature can contribute to tooth enamel erosion with frequent consumption.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Carbonated drinks may cause bloating or stomach discomfort in some individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled as a standalone beverage or use in non‑alcoholic cocktails. Adding a slice of lemon or lime can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within a few days.

content.title: About
content.content: Soybean curd, deep fried, consists of bite‑size pieces of tofu that are quickly fried until a golden, crispy crust forms. The interior remains soft and retains the mild, nutty flavor of soy. It is a common component in Asian cuisines, served as a snack or added to stir‑fries, soups, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tofu is made by coagulating soy milk and pressing the curds into blocks.
Deep‑fried tofu is known as “age‑dofu” in Japan and “zha doufu” (炸豆腐) in China.
The crispy exterior can hold sauces, making it a versatile vehicle for flavor.
Tofu provides a complete plant protein, making it popular among vegetarians and vegans.
When fried at the right temperature, the crust stays crunchy while the inside stays moist.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Tofu supplies all essential amino acids, supporting muscle maintenance and overall nutrition.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with animal proteins, tofu contains mostly polyunsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of calcium and iron
items.content: Coagulating agents such as calcium sulfate increase the calcium content; soy also provides iron.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Tofu is easy to digest and can be part of a diet that promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: It does not cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, making it suitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals with soy allergy may experience reactions ranging from mild to severe.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytates can bind minerals and reduce their absorption; soaking or fermenting tofu lowers this effect.

items.title: Oxalate levels
items.content: Tofu contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Frying oil considerations
items.content: Deep frying adds extra calories and can produce harmful compounds if the oil is overheated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Deep‑fried tofu can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed in salads, added to soups, stir‑fries, rice bowls, or used in wraps and sushi rolls. Drizzle with soy sauce, sprinkle with scallions, sesame seeds, or chili flakes for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried tofu in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze it; frozen pieces retain texture and flavor for about 2 months. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Winter squash is a variety that matures in the autumn‑winter period. A squash soufflé is a light, airy dish made from pureed squash, eggs, and a small amount of cream. It has a delicate sweet‑spicy flavor and a characteristic creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Squash belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family and is related to cucumber, zucchini, and melon.
Winter squash can be stored for several months under proper conditions, making it popular in the cold season.
Soufflé originated in France in the 17th century as a way to use egg whites for a light texture.
Squash is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A.
Pumpkin seeds left after preparation are often used in baking or as a snack.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene from squash supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C enhances antioxidant protection and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Squash soufflé, when made with moderate sugar and fat, fits well into a calorie‑controlled diet.

items.title: Fiber for digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Potassium for cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Squash allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to squash or its seeds.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Soufflé is often sweetened; people with diabetes should monitor sugar intake.

items.title: Added fats
items.content: Some recipes use butter or cream, increasing saturated fat levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm squash soufflé is served as a dessert, often topped with cinnamon, nuts, or caramel. It can be folded into layered cakes, muffins, or used as a filling for pancakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the finished soufflé in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen soufflé keeps well for up to 2 months; thaw it in the fridge and gently reheat before serving.

vegetable-and-fruit-juice-drink-with-hig.title: Vegetable and Fruit Juice Drink with High Vitamin C

content.title: About
content.content: The vegetable and fruit juice drink is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from a blend of fresh vegetables and fruits, fortified with vitamin C. It contains no added sugar, fits a diet plan, and easily integrates into daily nutrition.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Combining vegetables and fruits provides a broad spectrum of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants.
Vitamin C is stabilized to retain its activity even after extended storage.
The drink is often used in sports nutrition for rapid recovery after exercise.
Its low calorie content makes it popular among weight‑conscious consumers.
Manufacturers frequently add lime or lemon extract to boost flavor and vitamin C levels.

items.title: High vitamin C content
items.content: Vitamin C supports immune function, collagen synthesis, and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids from the fruits and vegetables help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: The drink provides a substantial amount of water and electrolytes, aiding fluid balance.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Absence of added sugar makes it suitable for diet regimens.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Fiber from the fruit and vegetable blend promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Allergy to specific ingredients
items.content: The beverage may contain fruits or vegetables that trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis.

items.title: Added sugar in some variants
items.content: Certain versions may contain added sugar; always check the label.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume the drink chilled as a refreshing snack, post‑workout recovery, or alongside a light breakfast. It can also be blended into smoothies or used as a base for cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not freeze, as this may alter taste and texture.
